name: The Five Phases
title: The Five Phases
answer: The Five Phases is a staged method for adopting AI in a school: assess readiness, choose the pilot, set up governance, run and evaluate, and scale what works. Each phase ends with a deliverable a leader can hold, and skipping a phase is the most common way a promising tool becomes an expensive disappointment. It matters because it gives schools a repeatable path from interest to adoption, with the pace set by how high the stakes are.

sections.body: The idea is a five phase sequence for bringing an AI tool into a school, with every phase producing something concrete rather than a vague sense of progress. The phases are assessing readiness, choosing the pilot, setting up governance, running and evaluating, and scaling what works. The problem it solves is the common pattern where a promising tool is adopted enthusiastically and then quietly fails, often because a step was skipped. The book states that skipping a phase is the most common way a promising tool turns into an expensive disappointment. Figure 4.2 lists each phase alongside its deliverable and its owner, so responsibility is visible at every stage.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or district, the phases are worked through in order, and the pace is matched to risk. A small district can move through the first three phases in a month for a low risk tool such as a lesson planning assistant. A tool that touches student records or decisions about students deserves more time at every step. The book's rule of thumb is that the higher the stakes, the slower the phases. The text does not give separate grade band guidance, so the same sequence applies across a school, with the stakes of the tool setting the speed.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or finding for this idea beyond the structure itself and the reference to Figure 4.2, which lists each phase with its deliverable and owner. The claim that skipping a phase is the most common way a promising tool turns into an expensive disappointment is presented as the book's own guidance rather than as research evidence. This idea therefore rests on practice rather than research as far as the supplied text shows.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main limit is pace: the phases should not be rushed when the tool is high stakes. The book draws the line at tools that touch student records or decisions about students, which deserve more time at every step, while a low risk tool such as a lesson planning assistant can move faster. The decision about how fast to go stays with the leader, guided by the rule that higher stakes mean slower phases. Each phase also has a named owner and a deliverable, so the work does not proceed without someone accountable for it. Nothing in the text removes human judgement from these choices.
